message.content: Read redu.md and deploy AliasVault on redu.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- amazon-bedrock: Builds generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock. Covers model invocation (Converse API, InvokeModel), RAG with Knowledge Bases, Bedrock Agents, Guardrails, and AgentCore. Use when invoking models, setting up Knowledge Bases, creating agents, applying guardrails, deploying to AgentCore, troubleshooting Bedrock errors (ThrottlingException, AccessDeniedException), or choosing models (Claude, Llama, [infra], Titan). ALSO USE for prompt caching setup and debugging, quota health checks and throttling diagnosis, cost attribution and tracking, migrating between Claude model generations (4.5 to 4.6 to 4.7), chunking strategies, API selection (Converse vs InvokeModel), guardrail capabilities, and model selection. Also covers AgentCore Payments setup (x402, microtransactions, Payment Manager, Connector, Instrument, Coinbase CDP, Stripe Privy, 402 Payment Required, pay for content, paid endpoint, agent payments). NOT for custom model training, Rekognition, or Comprehend.
- aws-billing-and-cost-management: Analyze AWS costs, find savings, manage budgets, evaluate Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, right-size EC2/Lambda/RDS/EBS with Compute Optimizer, look up service pricing, query CUR with Athena, detect cost anomalies, scope costs to billing views, and monitor Free Tier usage. Triggers on: AWS bill, cost analysis, reduce spend, savings plan, reserved instance, right-size, budget alert, cost optimization, pricing, free tier, cost anomaly, CUR, cost audit, billing view, billing view ARN.
- aws-blocks: Guides building full-stack applications with AWS Blocks — an Infrastructure-from-Code framework. Applies when creating APIs, selecting Building Blocks (KVStore, DistributedTable, Database, AuthBasic, AuthCognito, Realtime, AsyncJob, FileBucket, etc.), running local development, or deploying AWS Blocks applications. Also covers AWS Blocks topics with validated, version-specific patterns that prevent common mistakes. Triggers when user mentions AWS Blocks; project has aws-blocks/ directory; code imports @aws-blocks packages.
- aws-cdk: Authors, deploys, and troubleshoots AWS infrastructure using CDK with TypeScript or Python. Covers best practices, stack architecture, and construct patterns. Always use when writing CDK constructs, bootstrapping environments, running cdk deploy/synth/diff, fixing CDK or CloudFormation errors, planning stack structure, importing existing resources, resolving drift, or refactoring stacks without resource replacement.
- aws-cloudformation: Author, validate, and troubleshoot AWS CloudFormation templates. Covers template authoring with secure defaults, pre-deployment validation (cfn-lint, cfn-guard, change sets), and root-cause diagnosis of failed stacks using CloudFormation events and CloudTrail correlation.
- aws-containers: Deploys and operates containerized workloads on ECS, Fargate, and ECR. Covers task definitions, Fargate services, ECR repository setup and lifecycle policies, ECS Exec debugging, service scaling, deployment strategies, load balancer integration, and logging configuration. Use when deploying, debugging, or optimizing containers on AWS. ALSO USE for container deployment options (ECS vs ECS Express Mode), networking modes, health check troubleshooting, OOM errors, secrets injection, blue/green deployments, ECR image management, and App Runner sunset guidance and migration. NOT for Kubernetes, EKS, or CI/CD pipelines.
- aws-messaging-and-streaming: Guides use of AWS messaging and streaming services. Covers Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon MQ, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK). Use when implementing messaging and streaming patterns.
- aws-observability: Builds, configures, debugs, and optimizes AWS observability with CloudWatch (Log Insights, Metrics, Alarms, Dashboards, EMF), X-Ray, CloudTrail, and ADOT (AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry), AND enables/onboards services to Application Signals using ADOT auto-instrumentation SDKs. Covers Log Insights queries, alarms (metric, composite, anomaly), dashboards, custom metrics/EMF, X-Ray tracing and sampling, ADOT collector config, CloudTrail auditing, and end-to-end Application Signals enablement via ADOT SDKs (CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, CloudWatch Agent IAM, OTLP endpoints, ServiceEvents, Dynamic Instrumentation), breakpoint and snapshot in Dynamic Instrumentation, live data capture in running service, debug without redeploying. Applies to CloudWatch, alarms, dashboards, EMF, X-Ray, traces, CloudTrail,  ADOT, monitoring, synthetics/canaries, OR enabling/onboarding/instrumenting a service for Application Signals. Not for app logging or security threat detection.
- aws-sdk-js-v3-usage: AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 development patterns. Use when writing JavaScript or TypeScript code that uses AWS services via @aws-sdk/* packages (aws-sdk-js-v3), or when asked about schemas, runtime validation, serialization, or code generation in the context of the JS/TS AWS SDK.
- aws-sdk-python-usage: AWS SDK for Python (boto3/botocore) development patterns. You MUST use this skill when writing Python code that uses AWS services via boto3 or botocore. This includes creating service clients or resources, configuring sessions and credentials, handling errors with ClientError, using paginators and waiters, S3 file transfers and presigned URLs, DynamoDB table operations, and any boto3/botocore client configuration. Use this skill whenever Python code imports boto3 or botocore, or when the user asks about AWS operations in Python.
- aws-sdk-swift-usage: AWS SDK for Swift development patterns. Use when writing Swift code that uses AWS services via aws-sdk-swift package.
- aws-serverless: Builds, deploys, manages, debugs, configures, and optimizes serverless applications on AWS using Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, EventBridge, and SAM/CDK. Covers cold starts, CORS debugging, event source mappings, troubleshooting, concurrency, SnapStart, Powertools, function URLs, EventBridge Scheduler, Lambda layers, and production readiness. Triggers on mentions of Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, SAM templates, CDK serverless stacks, DynamoDB stream triggers, SQS event sources, cold starts, timeouts, 502/504 errors, throttling, concurrency, CORS, Powertools, or any event-driven architecture on AWS, even without the word "serverless." Does not apply to EC2, ECS/Fargate containers, or Amplify hosting.
- cso: Chief Security Officer mode. (gstack)
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- investigate: Systematic debugging with root cause investigation. (gstack)
- office-hours: YC Office Hours — two modes. (gstack)
- review: Pre-landing PR review. (gstack)
- signing-in-to-aws: Gets AWS credentials for CLI/SDK access via `aws login`. Activates when a developer needs to authenticate to AWS for local development, when an AWS operation fails due to missing or expired credentials, or when someone asks about setting up AWS access. Triggers: "set up AWS", "configure AWS", "aws login", "get credentials", "authenticate", "session expired", "token expired", "no credentials", "AccessDeniedException" with no configured credentials.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text: I'll start by reading redu.md to understand the deployment context.

content.content:
1	---
2	redu_schema: 2
3	repo: https://github.com/aliasvault/aliasvault
4	plan:
5	  tool: deploy_compose
6	  image: ghcr.io/aliasvault/aliasvault:0.30.4
7	  port: 80
8	  vm: m1.medium
9	  flavor_id: "3"
10	  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
11	  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
12	bootstrap:
13	  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
14	  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
15	  source: aliasvault
16	quirks:
17	  - "⛔⛔ SAY THIS TO THE USER BEFORE YOU PLAN ANYTHING, BECAUSE IT DECIDES WHETHER THEY WANT THE DEPLOY AT ALL. AliasVault is a password manager AND an email-alias service with its own inbound SMTP server. On redu you get the password manager in full, and the alias feature ONLY in its public form. Private email domains need ports 25 and 587 reachable from the internet plus an MX record and a matching PTR; redu proxies ONE HTTP port on a *.redu.cloud hostname and gives you no control of reverse DNS, so that half cannot work here and no configuration fixes it. Upstream is clear about both sides: docs/docs/installation/index.mdx:144 lists 25 and 587 as optional and only for private email domains, and the docker-compose install guide says that if you skip the email server setup AliasVault falls back to the public SpamOK domains. Those are FULLY PUBLIC by design: their own page says anyone who knows the alias can read its mail. So: vault private, aliases disposable rather than private. If the user came for the private mail server, stop here and tell them to use a host where they control port 25 and reverse DNS."
18	  - "USE THE ALL-IN-ONE IMAGE, NOT THE REPOSITORY ROOT COMPOSE FILE. docker-compose.yml at the repo root is the install.sh stack: seven services, its own bundled Postgres, its own nginx binding 80 AND 443, a certbot companion in docker-compose.letsencrypt.yml, and SMTP publishing 25 and 587. On redu that fights the platform at three points, since redu already terminates TLS and issues the certificate. The supported single-container path is ghcr.io/aliasvault/aliasvault, documented at docs/docs/installation/docker-compose/index.md, and it is the one this recipe uses. Pin it: 0.30.4 was the newest tag in the registry on 2026-08-17 and there is no v prefix. Never a rolling tag."
19	  - "⛔⛔ THE SILENT ONE: POSTGRES_HOST DEFAULTS TO localhost INSIDE THE IMAGE, SO A FORGOTTEN VARIABLE MEANS A HEALTHY INSTANCE ON THE WRONG DATABASE. Dockerfile:217-231 ships POSTGRES_HOST=localhost, POSTGRES_PORT=5432, POSTGRES_USER=aliasvault and POSTGRES_DATABASE=aliasvault as image defaults, and the container also runs its own PostgreSQL under s6. If your compose fails to pass POSTGRES_HOST, or the variable does not interpolate, AliasVault comes up perfectly healthy, serves the web app, accepts registrations and writes every vault into the container-local cluster under /database. Nothing errors. The managed database you are paying for stays empty. Set all four variables from redu's injected PGHOST, PGPORT, PGDATABASE and PGUSER, and prove it after boot with the script in this file, which checks the value AND counts the migration rows on the managed database."
20	  - "⛔⛔ THE DATABASE PASSWORD IS READ FROM A FILE, NOT FROM AN ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE. This is the single thing most likely to break a first attempt. PostgresqlDbContextFactory.cs:114-135 reads $SECRETS_PATH/postgres_password (default /secrets/postgres_password) and throws KeyNotFoundException if it is missing or empty; there is no POSTGRES_PASSWORD variable anywhere. Worse, init/script:44-50 GENERATES a random one into that path when the file is absent, so an unattended first boot invents a password that the managed database has never heard of. redu only ever hands you PGPASSWORD in the project .env, so the compose in this file runs a tiny busybox service FIRST that writes that value into ./secrets/postgres_password, and the app container waits on it with condition: service_completed_successfully. Write it on EVERY start, not only when absent, so a rotated database password heals itself."
21	  - "THE BUNDLED POSTGRES STILL RUNS EVEN WITH AN EXTERNAL DATABASE, AND THE API WAITS FOR IT. Upstream documents the first half (the database page says the embedded server keeps running but serves no connections), and api/run:9-28 is the half nobody documents: the API service loops for 60 seconds waiting for a psql connection to 127.0.0.1 as user aliasvault BEFORE it starts, whatever POSTGRES_HOST says, using the same password file. It works because the init script sets the local role's password from that same file. Two consequences: keep the /database volume mounted or the bundled cluster re-initialises on every boot and costs you a minute of startup, and do not be alarmed that /database fills with a cluster you are not using."
22	  - "⛔ THE SECRETS DIRECTORY IS WHAT A REDEPLOY DESTROYS, AND IT DOES NOT ERROR WHEN IT IS GONE. init/script:44-66 creates three files under $SECRETS_PATH only if each is absent: postgres_password, jwt_key and data_protection_cert_pass. reset-admin-password.sh adds a fourth, admin_password_hash. Lose that directory and the container regenerates them silently: every signed-in session and refresh token is invalidated by the new jwt_key, the ASP.NET data protection material no longer opens, and your admin login stops existing. The vaults themselves are end-to-end encrypted under each user's own master password, so they survive as long as the DATABASE does, which is the reason this recipe puts the database on a managed Postgres rather than in the container. Mount ./secrets on the persistent volume, keep it off any public path, and never commit it."
23	  - "⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: NOBODY, UNTIL YOU DO IT BY HAND, AND THAT IS THE GOOD NEWS. There is no default admin password and no first-visitor claim on the admin panel. StartupTasks.cs:47-52 skips creating the admin user entirely while no password hash is configured, and init/script:68-70 says so in the boot log. So /admin exists on the public hostname but has no account to sign into. YOU create it after boot with `sudo docker exec -it aliasvault aliasvault reset-admin-password -y`, which prints a generated password ONCE and writes only its hash to $SECRETS_PATH/admin_password_hash; then restart the container, because StartupTasks only reads that file at startup. Hand the password to the user in the session and never write it into this file or the deploy log. The admin panel does NOT hold anyone's vault contents; it is server administration, users, logs and email domains."
24	  - "⛔ THE VAULT SIGN-UP FORM IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION, AND IT IS OPEN ON FIRST BOOT. PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_ENABLED defaults to true in the image, and AuthController.cs:451-458 gates registration on that flag alone: there is NO first-user exemption, so the first account is not special and creating one does not close anything. Between the hostname going live and you turning the flag off, any stranger who finds the URL can create a vault on your instance. They do not become an administrator and they cannot read your vault (it is end-to-end encrypted), but they get storage on a machine you pay for and a row in your database. So: deploy with registration ON, create YOUR account in the browser straight away, then set PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_ENABLED to \"false\" and recreate the container, and confirm it with the script in this file. There is an IP-based registration rate limit (AuthController.cs:468-475) but it is a speed bump, not a lock."
25	  - "PORT 80, AND DO NOT PUBLISH ANYTHING ELSE. The image exposes 80, 443, 25 and 587. Publish ONLY 80 to the host and pass port 80 to deploy_compose: redu terminates TLS at its own proxy and issues the certificate, so the container's self-signed 443 listener is useless and its SMTP ports have nowhere to receive from. Leave FORCE_HTTPS_REDIRECT at \"false\"; nginx/run:23-30 defaults it to false in this image, but the multi-container .env.example says its default is true, so set it explicitly rather than trusting either. Setting it to true makes nginx serve 443 only and redu's proxy then gets nothing on 80."
26	  - "DO NOT SET ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST TO private. It reads like the safe choice and it locks YOU out. nginx/run:52-81 turns \"private\" into default-deny with only loopback and RFC1918 carved out, and behind redu's proxy the address being matched is the real client IP taken from X-Forwarded-For, which for you is a public address. The result is that /admin quietly serves the ordinary client app to everyone including its owner, with no error to explain it. Either leave ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST empty and rely on the admin password plus its lockout after repeated failures, or set it to the user's own public IP or CIDR, which they have to give you."
27	  - "THE DATABASE CONNECTION HAS NO SSL SETTING YOU CAN REACH. PostgresqlDbContextFactory.cs:59-76 builds the connection string from exactly five fields, Host, Database, Username, Port and the password from the file, and adds only KeepAlive and ConnectionIdleLifetime. There is no environment variable for sslmode, and the ConnectionStrings__AliasServerDbContext variable you might reach for is overridden whenever the app detects it is in a container. Traffic to the managed database stays on redu's private network between two VMs in the same project, which is what makes that acceptable; say so in the handover rather than implying the hop is TLS."
28	  - "VOLUMES: /database, /logs, /secrets and /certificates. The image itself declares VOLUME for the first three, so if you do not mount them Docker creates anonymous volumes and the next redeploy silently starts from nothing. /certificates only holds a self-signed pair that redu makes irrelevant, but mount it anyway so the container does not regenerate a 2048-bit RSA key on every boot. The one that MUST persist is /secrets; the one that holds real data, once this recipe is wired correctly, is the managed database rather than /database."
29	  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO FIGURE FOR THIS IMAGE. The install FAQ gives a whole-product minimum of 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM and 16 GB disk. One all-in-one container runs nginx, a full PostgreSQL 16 cluster and four .NET processes (api, admin, client, smtp) plus a task runner under s6, so m1.medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB / 40 GB) is the reasoning here, not a measurement. It is also the ceiling of redu's no-card trial, so it keeps this entry inside the trial. Measure it on the first real run and write the number back."
30	  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> tell the user the email caveat in the first quirk, show the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr, roughly GBP 33 a month, inside the no-card trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small), port 80. Do NOT pass db_superuser: the app creates no database of its own, it migrates into the one redu provisions. plan_deploy will want to upsize a compose stack to m1.large; pass flavor_id explicitly and hold m1.medium, since nothing here is built from source."
31	  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built. Write the two-service docker-compose.yml from this file locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. Cloning the upstream monorepo would fetch a mobile app, a browser extension and a docs site you will not use."
32	  - "AFTER THE FIRST ACCOUNT EXISTS, HAND OVER THE API URL, NOT JUST THE WEB URL. The browser extensions and the mobile apps connect to https://<your-host>/api, and the mobile apps enforce certificate validation at the OS level with no override, which is exactly why redu's real certificate matters here and a self-hosted self-signed one does not work. Give the user both URLs."
33	  - "LICENCE: GNU AGPL v3, read from LICENSE.md. awesome-selfhosted's metadata says MIT and it is WRONG. AGPL section 13 puts an obligation on whoever OPERATES the service: if you modify AliasVault and let other people use it over a network, those users must be offered the modified source. Deploying the unmodified official image for yourself or your team triggers nothing extra. Say this once in the handover; do not turn it into a legal opinion."
34	  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. The admin password from the reset script, the vault master password and the managed database password all belong to the user. Hand them over in the session. The deploy log records that an admin exists and that registration was closed, never the values."
35	  - "AFTERWARDS: pass THIS file to get_deployment as redu_md and write the merged redu_md_markdown back. Be aware that the merge refreshes the last_deploy block and appends a deploy-log line and does NOT write new quirks, so anything your run taught you has to be added by hand or it is lost."
36	  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM and its volume but keeps the managed Postgres, which is where the vaults are, and that database keeps billing at about GBP 0.0174/hr until delete_database. ⚠️ The VOLUME goes with the deployment, and the volume is where /secrets lives, so the jwt key, the data protection password and the admin password hash die with it even though the vault rows survive. Say that plainly before deleting anything."
37	---
38	
39	# Self-host AliasVault on redu
40	
41	An end-to-end encrypted password vault on a machine you own in the EU, with a managed Postgres
42	beside it and a real TLS certificate on a public hostname.
43	
44	## Read this before you deploy: the email half does not fully work here
45	
46	AliasVault is two things in one image. This is the honest split on redu:
47

quirks:
  - "⛔⛔ SAY THIS TO THE USER BEFORE YOU PLAN ANYTHING, BECAUSE IT DECIDES WHETHER THEY WANT THE DEPLOY AT ALL. AliasVault is a password manager AND an email-alias service with its own inbound SMTP server. On redu you get the password manager in full, and the alias feature ONLY in its public form. Private email domains need ports 25 and 587 reachable from the internet plus an MX record and a matching PTR; redu proxies ONE HTTP port on a *.redu.cloud hostname and gives you no control of reverse DNS, so that half cannot work here and no configuration fixes it. Upstream is clear about both sides: docs/docs/installation/index.mdx:144 lists 25 and 587 as optional and only for private email domains, and the docker-compose install guide says that if you skip the email server setup AliasVault falls back to the public SpamOK domains. Those are FULLY PUBLIC by design: their own page says anyone who knows the alias can read its mail. So: vault private, aliases disposable rather than private. If the user came for the private mail server, stop here and tell them to use a host where they control port 25 and reverse DNS."
  - "USE THE ALL-IN-ONE IMAGE, NOT THE REPOSITORY ROOT COMPOSE FILE. docker-compose.yml at the repo root is the install.sh stack: seven services, its own bundled Postgres, its own nginx binding 80 AND 443, a certbot companion in docker-compose.letsencrypt.yml, and SMTP publishing 25 and 587. The supported single-container path is ghcr.io/aliasvault/aliasvault, documented at docs/docs/installation/docker-compose/index.md, and it is the one this recipe uses. Pin it: 0.30.4 was the newest tag in the registry on 2026-08-17 and there is no v prefix. Never a rolling tag."
  - "⛔⛔ THE SILENT ONE: POSTGRES_HOST DEFAULTS TO localhost INSIDE THE IMAGE, SO A FORGOTTEN VARIABLE MEANS A HEALTHY INSTANCE ON THE WRONG DATABASE. If your compose fails to pass POSTGRES_HOST, or the variable does not interpolate, AliasVault comes up perfectly healthy, serves the web app, accepts registrations and writes every vault into the container-local cluster under /database. Nothing errors. The managed database you are paying for stays empty. Set all four variables from redu's injected PGHOST, PGPORT, PGDATABASE and PGUSER, and prove it after boot with the script in this file, which checks the value AND counts the migration rows on the managed database."
  - "⛔⛔ THE DATABASE PASSWORD IS READ FROM A FILE, NOT FROM AN ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE. This is the single thing most likely to break a first attempt. Worse, init/script:44-50 GENERATES a random one into that path when the file is absent, so an unattended first boot invents a password that the managed database has never heard of. redu only ever hands you PGPASSWORD in the project .env, so the compose in this file runs a tiny busybox service FIRST that writes that value into ./secrets/postgres_password, and the app container waits on it with condition: service_completed_successfully.   - "THE BUNDLED POSTGRES STILL RUNS EVEN WITH AN EXTERNAL DATABASE, AND THE API WAITS FOR IT. Upstream documents the first half (the database page says the embedded server keeps running but serves no connections), and api/run:9-28 is the half nobody documents: the API service loops for 60 seconds waiting for a psql connection to 127.0.0.1 as user aliasvault BEFORE it starts, whatever POSTGRES_HOST says, using the same password file. It works because the init script sets the local role's password from that same file. Two consequences: keep the /database volume mounted or the bundled cluster re-initialises on every boot and costs you a minute of startup, and do not be alarmed that /database fills with a cluster you are not using."
  - "⛔ THE SECRETS DIRECTORY IS WHAT A REDEPLOY DESTROYS, AND IT DOES NOT ERROR WHEN IT IS GONE. init/script:44-66 creates three files under $SECRETS_PATH only if each is absent: postgres_password, jwt_key and data_protection_cert_pass. reset-admin-password.sh adds a fourth, admin_password_hash. Lose that directory and the container regenerates them silently: every signed-in session and refresh token is invalidated by the new jwt_key, the ASP.NET data protection material no longer opens, and your admin login stops existing. The vaults themselves are end-to-end encrypted under each user's own master password, so they survive as long as the DATABASE does, which is the reason this recipe puts the database on a managed Postgres rather than in the container. Mount ./secrets on the persistent volume, keep it off any public path, and never commit it."
  - "⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: NOBODY, UNTIL YOU DO IT BY HAND, AND THAT IS THE GOOD NEWS. There is no default admin password and no first-visitor claim on the admin panel. StartupTasks.cs:47-52 skips creating the admin user entirely while no password hash is configured, and init/script:68-70 says so in the boot log. So /admin exists on the public hostname but has no account to sign into. YOU create it after boot with `sudo docker exec -it aliasvault aliasvault reset-admin-password -y`, which prints a generated password ONCE and writes only its hash to $SECRETS_PATH/admin_password_hash; then restart the container, because StartupTasks only reads that file at startup. Hand the password to the user in the session and never write it into this file or the deploy log. The admin panel does NOT hold anyone's vault contents; it is server administration, users, logs and email domains."
  - "⛔ THE VAULT SIGN-UP FORM IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION, AND IT IS OPEN ON FIRST BOOT. PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_ENABLED defaults to true in the image, and AuthController.cs:451-458 gates registration on that flag alone: there is NO first-user exemption, so the first account is not special and creating one does not close anything. Between the hostname going live and you turning the flag off, any stranger who finds the URL can create a vault on your instance. They do not become an administrator and they cannot read your vault (it is end-to-end encrypted), but they get storage on a machine you pay for and a row in your database. So: deploy with registration ON, create YOUR account in the browser straight away, then set PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_ENABLED to \"false\" and recreate the container, and confirm it with the script in this file. There is an IP-based registration rate limit (AuthController.cs:468-475) but it is a speed bump, not a lock."
  - "PORT 80, AND DO NOT PUBLISH ANYTHING ELSE. The image exposes 80, 443, 25 and 587. Publish ONLY 80 to the host and pass port 80 to deploy_compose: redu terminates TLS at its own proxy and issues the certificate, so the container's self-signed 443 listener is useless and its SMTP ports have nowhere to receive from. Leave FORCE_HTTPS_REDIRECT at \"false\"; nginx/run:23-30 defaults it to false in this image, but the multi-container .env.example says its default is true, so set it explicitly rather than trusting either. Setting it to true makes nginx serve 443 only and redu's proxy then gets nothing on 80."
  - "DO NOT SET ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST TO private. It reads like the safe choice and it locks YOU out. nginx/run:52-81 turns \"private\" into default-deny with only loopback and RFC1918 carved out, and behind redu's proxy the address being matched is the real client IP taken from X-Forwarded-For, which for you is a public address. The result is that /admin quietly serves the ordinary client app to everyone including its owner, with no error to explain it. Either leave ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST empty and rely on the admin password plus its lockout after repeated failures, or set it to the user's own public IP or CIDR, which they have to give you."
  - "THE DATABASE CONNECTION HAS NO SSL SETTING YOU CAN REACH. PostgresqlDbContextFactory.cs:59-76 builds the connection string from exactly five fields, Host, Database, Username, Port and the password from the file, and adds only KeepAlive and ConnectionIdleLifetime. There is no environment variable for sslmode, and the ConnectionStrings__AliasServerDbContext variable you might reach for is overridden whenever the app detects it is in a container. Traffic to the managed database stays on redu's private network between two VMs in the same project, which is what makes that acceptable; say so in the handover rather than implying the hop is TLS."
  - "VOLUMES: /database, /logs, /secrets and /certificates. The image itself declares VOLUME for the first three, so if you do not mount them Docker creates anonymous volumes and the next redeploy silently starts from nothing. /certificates only holds a self-signed pair that redu makes irrelevant, but mount it anyway so the container does not regenerate a 2048-bit RSA key on every boot. The one that MUST persist is /secrets; the one that holds real data, once this recipe is wired correctly, is the managed database rather than /database."
  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO FIGURE FOR THIS IMAGE. The install FAQ gives a whole-product minimum of 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM and 16 GB disk. One all-in-one container runs nginx, a full PostgreSQL 16 cluster and four .NET processes (api, admin, client, smtp) plus a task runner under s6, so m1.medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB / 40 GB) is the reasoning here, not a measurement. It is also the ceiling of redu's no-card trial, so it keeps this entry inside the trial. Measure it on the first real run and write the number back."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> tell the user the email caveat in the first quirk, show the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr, roughly GBP 33 a month, inside the no-card trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small), port 80. Cloning the upstream monorepo would fetch a mobile app, a browser extension and a docs site you will not use."
  - "AFTER THE FIRST ACCOUNT EXISTS, HAND OVER THE API URL, NOT JUST THE WEB URL. The browser extensions and the mobile apps connect to https://<your-host>/api, and the mobile apps enforce certificate validation at the OS level with no override, which is exactly why redu's real certificate matters here and a self-hosted self-signed one does not work. Give the user both URLs."

# Self-host AliasVault on redu

An end-to-end encrypted password vault on a machine you own in the EU, with a managed Postgres
beside it and a real TLS certificate on a public hostname.

## Read this before you deploy: the email half does not fully work here

AliasVault is two things in one image. This is the honest split on redu:

| | On redu |
|---|---|
| Password vault, browser extensions, mobile apps | **Works fully.** End-to-end encrypted, your own server. |
| Email aliases on **public** SpamOK domains | **Works.** Disposable, and public by design: anyone who knows the alias can read its mail. |
| Email aliases on **your own private domain** | **Does not work.** Needs inbound SMTP on ports 25 and 587, an MX record and a matching PTR. |

redu gives you one proxied HTTP port on a `*.redu.cloud` hostname with TLS, and no control over
reverse DNS. Upstream calls the mail server optional and documents the SpamOK fallback itself, so
this is a supported configuration and not a hack, but it is a smaller product than the one on
their front page. If private aliases are why you are here, use a host where you control port 25.

## What this deploys

- **AliasVault** from the official all-in-one image, pinned, on one m1.medium VM, port 80.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so the vaults survive a redeploy of the app.
- A volume holding `/secrets`, `/database`, `/logs` and `/certificates`.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS, which is what the mobile apps require.

About GBP 0.045/hour, roughly GBP 33 a month. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy AliasVault on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The compose file

Two services. The first exists only to put redu's database password where AliasVault actually
looks for it, which is a file and not an environment variable.

```yaml
services:
  secrets-init:
    image: busybox:1.38.0
    environment:
      PGPASSWORD: [REDACTED:value]}
    volumes:
      - ./secrets:«REDACTED:assigned:983a7415»
    command:
      - sh
      - -c
      - mkdir -p /secrets && printf '%s' "$$PGPASSWORD" > /secrets/postgres_password && chmod 600 /secrets/postgres_password

  aliasvault:
    image: ghcr.io/aliasvault/aliasvault:0.30.4
    container_name: aliasvault
    restart: unless-stopped
    depends_on:
      secrets-init:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    ports:
      - "80:80"
    environment:
      FORCE_HTTPS_REDIRECT: "false"
      PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_ENABLED: "true"
      ALIASVAULT_VERBOSITY: "1"
      POSTGRES_HOST: ${PGHOST}
      POSTGRES_PORT: ${PGPORT}
      POSTGRES_DATABASE: ${PGDATABASE}
      POSTGRES_USER: ${PGUSER}
    volumes:
      - ./database:/database
      - ./logs:/logs
      - ./secrets:«REDACTED:assigned:983a7415»
      - ./certificates:/certificates
```

The doubled `$$` in the busybox command is deliberate: a single `$` would be substituted by
Compose while it parses the file, which would bake the password into the container's command line
where `ps` and `docker inspect` can read it. Doubled, the shell inside the container expands it
from its own environment instead.

## Prove the vaults landed on the managed database

The failure this catches is the quiet one: `POSTGRES_HOST` defaults to `localhost` in the image,
so a missing variable gives you a perfectly healthy AliasVault writing into a Postgres inside the
container while the managed database you are paying for stays empty. Both halves are here: the
first command prints a value, which is what proves the command ran at all, and the second counts
rows that can only exist if the app migrated into the managed database.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
C=aliasvault
PSQL=/usr/lib/postgresql/16/bin/psql

host=$(sudo docker exec "$C" printenv POSTGRES_HOST 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r')
if [ -z "$host" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: could not read POSTGRES_HOST from the container"; exit 3
fi
echo "POSTGRES_HOST=$host"
if [ "$host" = "localhost" ] || [ "$host" = "127.0.0.1" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: AliasVault is using the Postgres bundled inside the container"; exit 1
fi

rows=$(sudo docker exec "$C" sh -c 'PGPASSWORD=[REDACTED:value] "$SECRETS_PATH/postgres_password") '"$PSQL"' -h "$POSTGRES_HOST" -p "$POSTGRES_PORT" -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DATABASE" -tAc "select count(*) from \"__EFMigrationsHistory\""' 2>&1 | tr -d '[:space:]')
echo "migrations applied on the managed database: $rows"
case "$rows" in
  ''|*[!0-9]*) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: that query did not return a number, so nothing above is proven"; exit 3 ;;
esac
if [ "$rows" -ge 1 ]; then
  echo "OK: the AliasVault schema is on the managed database"
else
  echo "FAIL: the managed database has no AliasVault schema"; exit 1
fi
```

## Close the sign-up form, then prove it is closed

Create your own vault in the browser first: with registration disabled there is no way to make
the first account, because AliasVault has no first-user exemption. Then set
`PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_ENABLED` to `"false"` in the compose file, recreate the container, and run
this.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
HOST=${1:-}
if [ -z "$HOST" ]; then echo "usage: $0 <your-host>.redu.cloud"; exit 2; fi
url="https://$HOST/api/v1/Auth/validate-username"
out=$(mktemp)

code=$(printf '%s' '{"username":""}' \
  | curl -sS -m 20 -o "$out" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @- "$url")
echo "HTTP $code"

if [ "$code" = "502" ] || [ "$code" = "503" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: still starting. redu answers 502 for the first couple of minutes. Re-run."
  rm -f "$out"; exit 3
fi

# The positive half. Either code proves we are talking to the AliasVault API and not to an error
# page, which is what makes the assertion below mean anything.
if ! grep -qE 'PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_DISABLED|USERNAME_REQUIRED' "$out"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: this is not an AliasVault API response. First 300 bytes:"
  head -c 300 "$out"; echo; rm -f "$out"; exit 3
fi

if grep -q 'PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_DISABLED' "$out"; then
  echo "OK: public registration is CLOSED"
  rm -f "$out"; exit 0
fi

echo "WARNING: public registration is still OPEN. Anyone who finds this hostname can create a"
echo "vault on it. Set PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_ENABLED to false and recreate the container."
rm -f "$out"; exit 1
```

## Create the admin account

There is no default admin password and no admin user at all until you make one. The panel at
`/admin` is on the public hostname from the moment the deploy is healthy, with nothing to sign
into, which is the safe state. Claim it:

```bash
sudo docker exec -it aliasvault aliasvault reset-admin-password -y
sudo docker restart aliasvault
```

The password is printed once and only its hash is written to `/secrets/admin_password_hash`. The
restart matters: the hash is only read at startup.

---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/aliasvault/aliasvault
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: ghcr.io/aliasvault/aliasvault:0.30.4
  port: 80
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: aliasvault
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔ SAY THIS TO THE USER BEFORE YOU PLAN ANYTHING, BECAUSE IT DECIDES WHETHER THEY WANT THE DEPLOY AT ALL. AliasVault is a password manager AND an email-alias service with its own inbound SMTP server. On redu you get the password manager in full, and the alias feature ONLY in its public form. Private email domains need ports 25 and 587 reachable from the internet plus an MX record and a matching PTR; redu proxies ONE HTTP port on a *.redu.cloud hostname and gives you no control of reverse DNS, so that half cannot work here and no configuration fixes it. Upstream is clear about both sides: docs/docs/installation/index.mdx:144 lists 25 and 587 as optional and only for private email domains, and the docker-compose install guide says that if you skip the email server setup AliasVault falls back to the public SpamOK domains. Those are FULLY PUBLIC by design: their own page says anyone who knows the alias can read its mail. So: vault private, aliases disposable rather than private. If the user came for the private mail server, stop here and tell them to use a host where they control port 25 and reverse DNS."
  - "USE THE ALL-IN-ONE IMAGE, NOT THE REPOSITORY ROOT COMPOSE FILE. docker-compose.yml at the repo root is the install.sh stack: seven services, its own bundled Postgres, its own nginx binding 80 AND 443, a certbot companion in docker-compose.letsencrypt.yml, and SMTP publishing 25 and 587. On redu that fights the platform at three points, since redu already terminates TLS and issues the certificate. The supported single-container path is ghcr.io/aliasvault/aliasvault, documented at docs/docs/installation/docker-compose/index.md, and it is the one this recipe uses. Pin it: 0.30.4 was the newest tag in the registry on 2026-08-17 and there is no v prefix. Never a rolling tag."
  - "⛔⛔ THE SILENT ONE: POSTGRES_HOST DEFAULTS TO localhost INSIDE THE IMAGE, SO A FORGOTTEN VARIABLE MEANS A HEALTHY INSTANCE ON THE WRONG DATABASE. Dockerfile:217-231 ships POSTGRES_HOST=localhost, POSTGRES_PORT=5432, POSTGRES_USER=aliasvault and POSTGRES_DATABASE=aliasvault as image defaults, and the container also runs its own PostgreSQL under s6. If your compose fails to pass POSTGRES_HOST, or the variable does not interpolate, AliasVault comes up perfectly healthy, serves the web app, accepts registrations and writes every vault into the container-local cluster under /database. Nothing errors. The managed database you are paying for stays empty. Set all four variables from redu's injected PGHOST, PGPORT, PGDATABASE and PGUSER, and prove it after boot with the script in this file, which checks the value AND counts the migration rows on the managed database."
  - "⛔⛔ THE DATABASE PASSWORD IS READ FROM A FILE, NOT FROM AN ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE. This is the single thing most likely to break a first attempt. PostgresqlDbContextFactory.cs:114-135 reads $SECRETS_PATH/postgres_password (default /secrets/postgres_password) and throws KeyNotFoundException if it is missing or empty; there is no POSTGRES_PASSWORD variable anywhere. Worse, init/script:44-50 GENERATES a random one into that path when the file is absent, so an unattended first boot invents a password that the managed database has never heard of. redu only ever hands you PGPASSWORD in the project .env, so the compose in this file runs a tiny busybox service FIRST that writes that value into ./secrets/postgres_password, and the app container waits on it with condition: service_completed_successfully. Write it on EVERY start, not only when absent, so a rotated database password heals itself."
  - "THE BUNDLED POSTGRES STILL RUNS EVEN WITH AN EXTERNAL DATABASE, AND THE API WAITS FOR IT. Upstream documents the first half (the database page says the embedded server keeps running but serves no connections), and api/run:9-28 is the half nobody documents: the API service loops for 60 seconds waiting for a psql connection to 127.0.0.1 as user aliasvault BEFORE it starts, whatever POSTGRES_HOST says, using the same password file. It works because the init script sets the local role's password from that same file. Two consequences: keep the /database volume mounted or the bundled cluster re-initialises on every boot and costs you a minute of startup, and do not be alarmed that /database fills with a cluster you are not using."
  - "⛔ THE SECRETS DIRECTORY IS WHAT A REDEPLOY DESTROYS, AND IT DOES NOT ERROR WHEN IT IS GONE. init/script:44-66 creates three files under $SECRETS_PATH only if each is absent: postgres_password, jwt_key and data_protection_cert_pass. reset-admin-password.sh adds a fourth, admin_password_hash. Lose that directory and the container regenerates them silently: every signed-in session and refresh token is invalidated by the new jwt_key, the ASP.NET data protection material no longer opens, and your admin login stops existing. The vaults themselves are end-to-end encrypted under each user's own master password, so they survive as long as the DATABASE does, which is the reason this recipe puts the database on a managed Postgres rather than in the container. Mount ./secrets on the persistent volume, keep it off any public path, and never commit it."
  - "⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: NOBODY, UNTIL YOU DO IT BY HAND, AND THAT IS THE GOOD NEWS. There is no default admin password and no first-visitor claim on the admin panel. StartupTasks.cs:47-52 skips creating the admin user entirely while no password hash is configured, and init/script:68-70 says so in the boot log. So /admin exists on the public hostname but has no account to sign into. YOU create it after boot with `sudo docker exec -it aliasvault aliasvault reset-admin-password -y`, which prints a generated password ONCE and writes only its hash to $SECRETS_PATH/admin_password_hash; then restart the container, because StartupTasks only reads that file at startup. Hand the password to the user in the session and never write it into this file or the deploy log. The admin panel does NOT hold anyone's vault contents; it is server administration, users, logs and email domains."
  - "⛔ THE VAULT SIGN-UP FORM IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION, AND IT IS OPEN ON FIRST BOOT. PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_ENABLED defaults to true in the image, and AuthController.cs:451-458 gates registration on that flag alone: there is NO first-user exemption, so the first account is not special and creating one does not close anything. Between the hostname going live and you turning the flag off, any stranger who finds the URL can create a vault on your instance. They do not become an administrator and they cannot read your vault (it is end-to-end encrypted), but they get storage on a machine you pay for and a row in your database. So: deploy with registration ON, create YOUR account in the browser straight away, then set PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_ENABLED to \"false\" and recreate the container, and confirm it with the script in this file. There is an IP-based registration rate limit (AuthController.cs:468-475) but it is a speed bump, not a lock."
  - "PORT 80, AND DO NOT PUBLISH ANYTHING ELSE. The image exposes 80, 443, 25 and 587. Publish ONLY 80 to the host and pass port 80 to deploy_compose: redu terminates TLS at its own proxy and issues the certificate, so the container's self-signed 443 listener is useless and its SMTP ports have nowhere to receive from. Leave FORCE_HTTPS_REDIRECT at \"false\"; nginx/run:23-30 defaults it to false in this image, but the multi-container .env.example says its default is true, so set it explicitly rather than trusting either. Setting it to true makes nginx serve 443 only and redu's proxy then gets nothing on 80."
  - "DO NOT SET ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST TO private. It reads like the safe choice and it locks YOU out. nginx/run:52-81 turns \"private\" into default-deny with only loopback and RFC1918 carved out, and behind redu's proxy the address being matched is the real client IP taken from X-Forwarded-For, which for you is a public address. The result is that /admin quietly serves the ordinary client app to everyone including its owner, with no error to explain it. Either leave ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST empty and rely on the admin password plus its lockout after repeated failures, or set it to the user's own public IP or CIDR, which they have to give you."
  - "THE DATABASE CONNECTION HAS NO SSL SETTING YOU CAN REACH. PostgresqlDbContextFactory.cs:59-76 builds the connection string from exactly five fields, Host, Database, Username, Port and the password from the file, and adds only KeepAlive and ConnectionIdleLifetime. There is no environment variable for sslmode, and the ConnectionStrings__AliasServerDbContext variable you might reach for is overridden whenever the app detects it is in a container. Traffic to the managed database stays on redu's private network between two VMs in the same project, which is what makes that acceptable; say so in the handover rather than implying the hop is TLS."
  - "VOLUMES: /database, /logs, /secrets and /certificates. The image itself declares VOLUME for the first three, so if you do not mount them Docker creates anonymous volumes and the next redeploy silently starts from nothing. /certificates only holds a self-signed pair that redu makes irrelevant, but mount it anyway so the container does not regenerate a 2048-bit RSA key on every boot. The one that MUST persist is /secrets; the one that holds real data, once this recipe is wired correctly, is the managed database rather than /database."
  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO FIGURE FOR THIS IMAGE. The install FAQ gives a whole-product minimum of 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM and 16 GB disk. One all-in-one container runs nginx, a full PostgreSQL 16 cluster and four .NET processes (api, admin, client, smtp) plus a task runner under s6, so m1.medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB / 40 GB) is the reasoning here, not a measurement. It is also the ceiling of redu's no-card trial, so it keeps this entry inside the trial. Measure it on the first real run and write the number back."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> tell the user the email caveat in the first quirk, show the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr, roughly GBP 33 a month, inside the no-card trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small), port 80. Do NOT pass db_superuser: the app creates no database of its own, it migrates into the one redu provisions. plan_deploy will want to upsize a compose stack to m1.large; pass flavor_id explicitly and hold m1.medium, since nothing here is built from source."
  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built. Write the two-service docker-compose.yml from this file locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. Cloning the upstream monorepo would fetch a mobile app, a browser extension and a docs site you will not use."
  - "AFTER THE FIRST ACCOUNT EXISTS, HAND OVER THE API URL, NOT JUST THE WEB URL. The browser extensions and the mobile apps connect to https://<your-host>/api, and the mobile apps enforce certificate validation at the OS level with no override, which is exactly why redu's real certificate matters here and a self-hosted self-signed one does not work. Give the user both URLs."
  - "LICENCE: GNU AGPL v3, read from LICENSE.md. awesome-selfhosted's metadata says MIT and it is WRONG. AGPL section 13 puts an obligation on whoever OPERATES the service: if you modify AliasVault and let other people use it over a network, those users must be offered the modified source. Deploying the unmodified official image for yourself or your team triggers nothing extra. Say this once in the handover; do not turn it into a legal opinion."
  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. The admin password from the reset script, the vault master password and the managed database password all belong to the user. Hand them over in the session. The deploy log records that an admin exists and that registration was closed, never the values."
  - "AFTERWARDS: pass THIS file to get_deployment as redu_md and write the merged redu_md_markdown back. Be aware that the merge refreshes the last_deploy block and appends a deploy-log line and does NOT write new quirks, so anything your run taught you has to be added by hand or it is lost."

# Self-host AliasVault on redu

An end-to-end encrypted password vault on a machine you own in the EU, with a managed Postgres
beside it and a real TLS certificate on a public hostname.

## Read this before you deploy: the email half does not fully work here

AliasVault is two things in one image. This is the honest split on redu:

| | On redu |
|---|---|
| Password vault, browser extensions, mobile apps | **Works fully.** End-to-end encrypted, your own server. |
| Email aliases on **public** SpamOK domains | **Works.** Disposable, and public by design: anyone who knows the alias can read its mail. |
| Email aliases on **your own private domain** | **Does not work.** Needs inbound SMTP on ports 25 and 587, an MX record and a matching PTR. |

redu gives you one proxied HTTP port on a `*.redu.cloud` hostname with TLS, and no control over
reverse DNS. Upstream calls the mail server optional and documents the SpamOK fallback itself, so
this is a supported configuration and not a hack, but it is a smaller product than the one on
their front page. If private aliases are why you are here, use a host where you control port 25.

## What this deploys

- **AliasVault** from the official all-in-one image, pinned, on one m1.medium VM, port 80.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so the vaults survive a redeploy of the app.
- A volume holding `/secrets`, `/database`, `/logs` and `/certificates`.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS, which is what the mobile apps require.

About GBP 0.045/hour, roughly GBP 33 a month. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy AliasVault on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The compose file

Two services. The first exists only to put redu's database password where AliasVault actually
looks for it, which is a file and not an environment variable.

```yaml
services:
  secrets-init:
    image: busybox:1.38.0
    environment:
      PGPASSWORD: [REDACTED:value]}
    volumes:
      - ./secrets:«REDACTED:assigned:983a7415»
    command:
      - sh
      - -c
      - mkdir -p /secrets && printf '%s' "$$PGPASSWORD" > /secrets/postgres_password && chmod 600 /secrets/postgres_password

  aliasvault:
    image: ghcr.io/aliasvault/aliasvault:0.30.4
    container_name: aliasvault
    restart: unless-stopped
    depends_on:
      secrets-init:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    ports:
      - "80:80"
    environment:
      FORCE_HTTPS_REDIRECT: "false"
      PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_ENABLED: "true"
      ALIASVAULT_VERBOSITY: "1"
      POSTGRES_HOST: ${PGHOST}
      POSTGRES_PORT: ${PGPORT}
      POSTGRES_DATABASE: ${PGDATABASE}
      POSTGRES_USER: ${PGUSER}
    volumes:
      - ./database:/database
      - ./logs:/logs
      - ./secrets:«REDACTED:assigned:983a7415»
      - ./certificates:/certificates
```

The doubled `$$` in the busybox command is deliberate: a single `$` would be substituted by
Compose while it parses the file, which would bake the password into the container's command line
where `ps` and `docker inspect` can read it. Doubled, the shell inside the container expands it
from its own environment instead.

## Prove the vaults landed on the managed database

The failure this catches is the quiet one: `POSTGRES_HOST` defaults to `localhost` in the image,
so a missing variable gives you a perfectly healthy AliasVault writing into a Postgres inside the
container while the managed database you are paying for stays empty. Both halves are here: the
first command prints a value, which is what proves the command ran at all, and the second counts
rows that can only exist if the app migrated into the managed database.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
C=aliasvault
PSQL=/usr/lib/postgresql/16/bin/psql

host=$(sudo docker exec "$C" printenv POSTGRES_HOST 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r')
if [ -z "$host" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: could not read POSTGRES_HOST from the container"; exit 3
fi
echo "POSTGRES_HOST=$host"
if [ "$host" = "localhost" ] || [ "$host" = "127.0.0.1" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: AliasVault is using the Postgres bundled inside the container"; exit 1
fi

rows=$(sudo docker exec "$C" sh -c 'PGPASSWORD=[REDACTED:value] "$SECRETS_PATH/postgres_password") '"$PSQL"' -h "$POSTGRES_HOST" -p "$POSTGRES_PORT" -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DATABASE" -tAc "select count(*) from \"__EFMigrationsHistory\""' 2>&1 | tr -d '[:space:]')
echo "migrations applied on the managed database: $rows"
case "$rows" in
  ''|*[!0-9]*) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: that query did not return a number, so nothing above is proven"; exit 3 ;;
esac
if [ "$rows" -ge 1 ]; then
  echo "OK: the AliasVault schema is on the managed database"
else
  echo "FAIL: the managed database has no AliasVault schema"; exit 1
fi
```

## Close the sign-up form, then prove it is closed

Create your own vault in the browser first: with registration disabled there is no way to make
the first account, because AliasVault has no first-user exemption. Then set
`PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_ENABLED` to `"false"` in the compose file, recreate the container, and run
this.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
HOST=${1:-}
if [ -z "$HOST" ]; then echo "usage: $0 <your-host>.redu.cloud"; exit 2; fi
url="https://$HOST/api/v1/Auth/validate-username"
out=$(mktemp)

code=$(printf '%s' '{"username":""}' \
  | curl -sS -m 20 -o "$out" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @- "$url")
echo "HTTP $code"

if [ "$code" = "502" ] || [ "$code" = "503" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: still starting. redu answers 502 for the first couple of minutes. Re-run."
  rm -f "$out"; exit 3
fi

# The positive half. Either code proves we are talking to the AliasVault API and not to an error
# page, which is what makes the assertion below mean anything.
if ! grep -qE 'PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_DISABLED|USERNAME_REQUIRED' "$out"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: this is not an AliasVault API response. First 300 bytes:"
  head -c 300 "$out"; echo; rm -f "$out"; exit 3
fi

if grep -q 'PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_DISABLED' "$out"; then
  echo "OK: public registration is CLOSED"
  rm -f "$out"; exit 0
fi

echo "WARNING: public registration is still OPEN. Anyone who finds this hostname can create a"
echo "vault on it. Set PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_ENABLED to false and recreate the container."
rm -f "$out"; exit 1
```

## Create the admin account

There is no default admin password and no admin user at all until you make one. The panel at
`/admin` is on the public hostname from the moment the deploy is healthy, with nothing to sign
into, which is the safe state. Claim it:

```bash
sudo docker exec -it aliasvault aliasvault reset-admin-password -y
sudo docker restart aliasvault
```

The password is printed once and only its hash is written to `/secrets/admin_password_hash`. The
restart matters: the hash is only read at startup.

Plan written to `redu-deploy-plan.md`. Here it is:

## Deployment plan — AliasVault on redu

```
user ──https──> <name>.redu.cloud  (redu proxy, real TLS cert)
                      │
        ┌─────────────┴──────────── your private network ────────────┐
        │  App VM ×1  m1.medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB / 40 GB)              │
        │  ghcr.io/aliasvault/aliasvault:0.30.4  — port 80 only      │
        │            │                                              │
        │            └──5432, private only──> Managed Postgres       │
        │                                     m1.small (1 vCPU/2 GB) │
        └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

| Resource | Rate | Monthly (~730h) |
|---|---|---|
| m1.medium — app VM | £0.0278/hr | £20.29 |
| m1.small — managed Postgres | £0.0174/hr | £12.70 |
| **Total** | **£0.0452/hr** | **£33.00/mo** |

Billed hourly, deletable any time, and inside the no-card free trial. Quota fits (2 instances, 3 vCPU, 6 GB against 10/20/50 available).

**One deviation worth flagging:** `plan_deploy` wanted to size the app VM at **m1.large** (£48.18/mo) because it raises multi-container compose stacks to a build-capable floor. Nothing here is built from source — it's one pinned prebuilt image plus a busybox one-shot — so I'm holding **m1.medium**, which is what redu.md records and what keeps this in the trial. That saves £15/mo. Note the m1.medium sizing is upstream-informed reasoning, not a measurement; I'll record the real figure after it runs.

**What happens after the VM is up**, so there are no surprises:
1. Verify the vaults actually landed on the *managed* database — the image silently defaults `POSTGRES_HOST` to `localhost`, which yields a perfectly healthy instance writing to the wrong place.
2. You create your vault account in the browser. Registration is **open** from the moment the hostname is live and there's no first-user exemption, so this happens promptly.
3. I close public registration and prove it's closed.
4. I create the admin account and hand you the generated password here in the session — never written to a file or log.

Also: this deploys **GNU AGPL v3** software (the awesome-selfhosted MIT metadata is wrong). Running the unmodified official image for yourself or your team triggers no extra obligation.

  ''|*[!0-9]*) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: that query did not return a number, so nothing above is proven"; exit 3 ;;
esac
if [ "$rows" -ge 1 ]; then
  echo "OK: the AliasVault schema is on the managed database"
else
  echo "FAIL: the managed database has no AliasVault schema"; exit 1
fi

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
HOST=${1:-}
if [ -z "$HOST" ]; then echo "usage: $0 <your-host>.redu.cloud"; exit 2; fi
url="https://$HOST/api/v1/Auth/validate-username"
out=$(mktemp)

code=$(printf '%s' '{"username":""}' \
  | curl -sS -m 20 -o "$out" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @- "$url")
echo "HTTP $code"

if [ "$code" = "502" ] || [ "$code" = "503" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: still starting. redu answers 502 for the first couple of minutes. Re-run."
  rm -f "$out"; exit 3
fi

# The positive half. Either code proves we are talking to the AliasVault API and not to an error
# page, which is what makes the assertion below mean anything.
if ! grep -qE 'PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_DISABLED|USERNAME_REQUIRED' "$out"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: this is not an AliasVault API response. First 300 bytes:"
  head -c 300 "$out"; echo; rm -f "$out"; exit 3
fi

if grep -q 'PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_DISABLED' "$out"; then
  echo "OK: public registration is CLOSED"
  rm -f "$out"; exit 0
fi

echo "WARNING: public registration is still OPEN. Anyone who finds this hostname can create a"
echo "vault on it. Set PUBLIC_REGISTRATION_ENABLED to false and recreate the container."
rm -f "$out"; exit 1
